entities.name: George Washington
entities.body: President of the Constitutional Convention and first President of the United States, cited for his conduct and his Farewell Address's foreign-policy maxims; bare "Washington" binds here as the dominant sense (see the namesake note above for the one place-reference to the city that shares the surname).

entities.name: Thomas Jefferson
entities.body: Cited repeatedly as an authority in his own right (his "Notes on Virginia"), as the third President, and for his letters to Madison and Lafayette on the instability of laws and on the loyalty of the Eastern states.

entities.name: Alexander Hamilton
entities.body: Named among the fifty-five Constitutional Convention delegates, among the three authors (with Jay and Madison) of The Federalist, and, per a footnote, one of the Constitution's principal founders.

entities.name: James Madison
entities.body: Named among the Convention delegates and Federalist authors, and cited for a letter from Jefferson to him on the instability of American laws and on executive power.

entities.name: John Jay
entities.body: Named as one of the three authors, with Hamilton and Madison, of The Federalist.

entities.name: William Penn
entities.body: Received by the Lenape a hundred and fifty years before Tocqueville's writing, on the banks of a river -- cited in the chapter on the fate of Native American tribes.

entities.name: Benjamin Franklin
entities.body: Cited for his own attempt to establish a single legislative House, and for his Autobiography as a source.

entities.name: James Monroe
entities.body: Named as the fourth of the early Presidents (with Washington, Jefferson, and Madison) associated with the Union's founding generation.

entities.name: John Quincy Adams
entities.body: "Mr. Quincy Adams," cited for dismissing federal officeholders on entering office in 1825 -- one of only two such wholesale removals Tocqueville could find before Jefferson's own in 1801.

entities.name: Andrew Jackson
entities.body: "General Jackson," twice elected President, cited for his restrained use of the removal power compared to his predecessor, and for his conduct in a public affair Tocqueville criticizes as "that of a heartless despot."

entities.name: James Buchanan
entities.body: Cited for retaining office, after Lincoln's election, from November 1860 to March 1861 -- a period Tocqueville's argument suggests could have enabled a dangerous abuse of power.

entities.name: Abraham Lincoln
entities.body: His 1860 election is cited as the point after which Buchanan remained in office; a separate translator's note observes that his election "was the signal of civil war," a later historical event Tocqueville's own text anticipates but does not narrate.

entities.name: Andrew Johnson
entities.body: His 1868 impeachment is cited in a bracketed translator's note as an example -- occurring after Tocqueville's own death -- of the kind of political crisis his analysis anticipated.

entities.name: John C. Calhoun
entities.body: Vice-President and head of the Southern nullification party, quoted for a sentence summarizing that party's position before the Senate.

entities.name: Henry Clay
entities.body: "Mr. Clay," credited with bringing in the bill (the Missouri Compromise) that passed both Houses of Congress within four days.

entities.name: Robert E. Lee
entities.body: "General Lee," cited in a bracketed translator's note on 1862 events as holding that his primary allegiance was owed to Virginia rather than to the Union -- illustrating, after the fact, the sectional loyalty Tocqueville's chapter describes.

entities.name: Benedict Arnold
entities.body: "The treacherous Arnold," invoked by an opposition faction as an insulting comparison for Washington's administration, per Marshall.

entities.name: Edward Everett
entities.body: "Mr. Edward Everett," cited for an 1830 statement to the House of Representatives on Native American population figures.

entities.name: Mr. Richards
entities.body: Mayor of Philadelphia, thanked by Tocqueville for supplying thirteen years of city budget figures.

entities.name: Chancellor Kent
entities.body: Author of the "Commentaries" cited constantly, alongside Story, as a legal authority throughout the Federal Constitution chapter's footnotes.

entities.name: Justice Joseph Story
entities.body: "Judge of the Supreme Court of the United States," author of the "Commentaries on the Constitution" cited even more frequently than Kent as the chapter's principal legal authority.

entities.name: Thomas Sergeant
entities.body: Cited for a work on the constitution and jurisdiction of the United States courts.

entities.name: Henry Wheaton
entities.body: Named with Kent and Story as an authority whose truthfulness on a particular point Tocqueville vouches for.

entities.name: Blackstone
entities.body: Cited, with Delolme, on a point of English constitutional law.

entities.name: Delolme
entities.body: Cited, with Blackstone, on English constitutional law.

entities.name: William Stith
entities.body: Author of a "History of Virginia" cited for the character of early Virginia's adventurer-colonists.

entities.name: Robert Beverley
entities.body: Author of another "History of Virginia, from the Earliest Period," cited alongside Stith and Jefferson's own "Notes."

entities.name: Nathaniel Morton
entities.body: "The historian of the first years of the settlement," cited for his account of the Plymouth colonists landing on a barren coast.

entities.name: Thomas Hutchinson
entities.body: Author of a "History of the Colony of Massachusetts Bay," cited repeatedly on early Massachusetts law and governance.

entities.name: Timothy Pitkin
entities.body: Author of a "History" cited repeatedly on colonial charters and the founding of several colonies.

entities.name: George Chalmers
entities.body: Cited (as printed, "Chalmer") for early Virginia's importation of enslaved people.

entities.name: Ebenezer Hazard
entities.body: Author of a 1792 historical documents collection cited for colonial records.

entities.name: Cotton Mather
entities.body: Author of "Magnalia Christi Americana," cited for a speech made by Winthrop defending himself against a charge of arbitrary conduct.

entities.name: John Winthrop
entities.body: Massachusetts colonial governor, whose self-defense against a charge of arbitrary conduct is quoted via Mather.

entities.name: Captain John Smith
entities.body: Author of a "History of Virginia, from the First Settlements in the year 1624," cited among the early colonial historians.

entities.name: John Marshall
entities.body: Author of a "Life of Washington" cited repeatedly, including for Washington's own letters and for the opposition's comparison of his administration to Benedict Arnold.

entities.name: Isaac Goodwin
entities.body: Author of "The Town-Officer" (Worcester, 1827), cited on New England town governance.

entities.name: Malte-Brun
entities.body: The geographer, cited repeatedly (as printed, without a hyphen, "Malte Brun") on Caribbean waters, American population density, and European emigration rates.

entities.name: William Darby
entities.body: Author of "View of the United States," cited repeatedly on American population and territory statistics.

entities.name: Alexander von Humboldt
entities.body: Cited, with Malte-Brun and Fischer, on the unresolved question of Native American origins.

entities.name: Fischer
entities.body: Author of a "Conjecture sur l'Origine des Americains," cited alongside Humboldt and Adair on Native American origins.

entities.name: James Adair
entities.body: Author of a "History of the American Indians," cited on Native American origins.

entities.name: Le Page du Pratz
entities.body: Author of "Histoire de la Louisiane" (printed "Lepage Dupratz"), cited among the sources for Native American history.

entities.name: Charlevoix
entities.body: Author of "Histoire de la Nouvelle France," cited repeatedly for early French colonial and Native American history.

entities.name: John Heckewelder
entities.body: The Moravian missionary (cited as printed, "Rev. G. Hecwelder"), whose letters on Native Americans are cited as a source.

entities.name: Volney
entities.body: Author of "Tableau des États-Unis," cited repeatedly (and by name, "M. de Volney") on Native American population decline and customs, from whom Tocqueville says he borrows some details directly.

entities.name: John Tanner
entities.body: A European carried off by Native Americans at age six, whose memoirs Tocqueville cites at length as evidence of Native American decline and hardship; Tocqueville reports having met him personally at Lake Superior.

entities.name: William Clark
entities.body: Co-author (with Cass) of an 1829 report to Congress on Native American affairs, quoted repeatedly on tribal displacement and customs.

entities.name: Lewis Cass
entities.body: Co-author (with Clark) of the same 1829 report; identified as "now the Secretary of War" at the time of Tocqueville's writing.

entities.name: Mr. Bell
entities.body: Author of an 1829 report to the Committee on Indian Affairs, cited independently on the pace of Native American displacement.

entities.name: Metacom
entities.body: The Wampanoag leader (called "King Philip" by the English), who led the confederated tribes' 1675 war against the New England colonists.

entities.name: René Descartes
entities.body: Cited repeatedly on method in philosophy, grouped with Bacon, Luther, and Voltaire as thinkers who broke from received authority -- though Tocqueville notes Americans read his method more than his books.

entities.name: Blaise Pascal
entities.body: Quoted four times across widely separated chapters -- on truth fleeing the mind's grasp, on the stakes of religious belief, and on the advantages of noble birth.

entities.name: Francis Bacon
entities.body: Named alongside Descartes as a great seventeenth-century method-reformer, this time in the natural sciences.

entities.name: Voltaire
entities.body: Grouped with Luther and Descartes as sharing a common method of breaking from inherited authority.

entities.name: Martin Luther
entities.body: Grouped with Descartes and Voltaire as a method-reformer; separately, Tocqueville speculates how he might have fared "in an age of equality."

entities.name: Montesquieu
entities.body: Cited three times: on absolute power's tendency to destroy religion, on despondency under the Roman Caesars, and on the nature of authority in societies without an intervening class.

entities.name: Plutarch
entities.body: Quoted three times: on Archimedes's lofty contempt for practical invention, on martial prowess in his "Life of Coriolanus," and for his "Lives of Great Commanders" as evidence of ancient military familiarity between officers and men.

entities.name: Montaigne
entities.body: Quoted on following "the straight road" rather than a winding one.

entities.name: Socrates
entities.body: Cited for the uncertain fixity of his and his followers' philosophical opinions.

entities.name: Cicero
entities.body: Cited for declaiming against the cruelty of crucifying a Roman citizen -- in contrast, per Tocqueville, to indifference toward the same cruelty inflicted on slaves.

entities.name: Machiavelli
entities.body: Quoted from "The Prince" on the greater difficulty of conducting protracted warfare among neighboring, formidable states.

entities.name: Archimedes
entities.body: Quoted via Plutarch for his lofty disdain of the merely practical uses of his inventions.

entities.name: Tacitus
entities.body: Cited for his description of ancient Germanic tribal customs, compared by Tocqueville to Native American customs he has personally observed.

entities.name: Aesop
entities.body: Named, with Terence, among distinguished ancient authors who were or had been enslaved.

entities.name: Terence
entities.body: Named with Aesop as a distinguished ancient author who had been enslaved.

entities.name: Aulus Gellius
entities.body: Cited via a quotation in Racine's preface to "Britannicus" on a point of Roman religious custom.

entities.name: Cabanis
entities.body: Cited for the view that thought is a secretion of the brain, which Tocqueville treats as one extreme of materialist philosophy.

entities.name: La Bruyère
entities.body: Cited (as printed, "Labruyere") for satirizing the vices and follies of his times while living within Louis XIV's own palace.

entities.name: Molière
entities.body: Named alongside La Bruyère for criticizing courtiers in plays performed before those same courtiers.

entities.name: Jean Racine
entities.body: Cited for his humble preface to "Britannicus," apologizing for a detail about the Vestal Junia's age.

entities.name: William Shakespeare
entities.body: Cited for the presence of his plays even in a frontier log-house, and for Tocqueville's own memory of reading "Henry V" there.

entities.name: John Milton
entities.body: Credited with introducing more than six hundred new words into the English language -- evidence, for Tocqueville, of an era before democratic language change slowed such invention.

entities.name: Jacques-Louis David
entities.body: The Neoclassical painter, contrasted with Raphael as a superior anatomist who depicted models with exact fidelity rather than idealizing them -- not the biblical King David, who is not otherwise named in this book; see the namesake note above.

entities.name: Raphael
entities.body: The painter, contrasted with David's group as pursuing an ideal beauty beyond mere anatomical accuracy.

entities.name: Napoleon
entities.body: Cited for causing jurors to be returned to service by his own agents (echoing an English royal practice), and, separately, as the reputed inventor of a new, more decisive system of warfare.

entities.name: Sulla
entities.body: Named with Caesar as an exemplar of seizing supreme power by force -- a generic historical byword, not a narrative reference to his own specific acts.

entities.name: Philip of Macedon
entities.body: Bare "Philip," cited for undertaking to execute the decree of the Amphictyons in ancient Greece -- distinct from the Wampanoag leader Metacom, whom the English called "King Philip" but who is never named "Philip" in this book itself; see the namesake note above.

entities.name: Henry IV of France
entities.body: Named alongside Louis XIV as a monarch whose absolute style of rule some hoped, mistakenly per Tocqueville, could be revived.

entities.name: Henry VIII
entities.body: Named with Elizabeth as an English monarch under whom, absent the civil jury, English liberty would have perished.

entities.name: Elizabeth I
entities.body: Named with Henry VIII as a monarch under whom the civil jury preserved English liberty in reality, if not always in law.

entities.name: Louis XIV
entities.body: Named alongside Henry IV as a monarch whose absolutism some hoped, mistakenly, to revive; also the monarch in whose palace La Bruyère lived while composing his satirical chapter on the great.

entities.name: Madame de Sévigné
entities.body: The letter-writer, quoted at length (as printed, "Sevigne") describing, to her daughter, a brutal punishment she witnessed with what Tocqueville stresses was not personal cruelty but a failure to extend full human sympathy across class lines.

entities.name: the Marquis de Lafayette
entities.body: Recipient of a Jefferson letter on wartime state loyalties, quoted directly; separately cited for his own "Memoirs."

entities.name: Margaret Bedford
entities.body: Convicted of "loose conduct" by a 1643 New Haven court and sentenced to be whipped and to marry her accomplice, Nicholas Jemmings -- cited as an example of colonial New England's moral-legislation severity.

entities.name: Nicholas Jemmings
entities.body: Margaret Bedford's accomplice, whom the same 1643 court sentence ordered her to marry.

coverage: A work of political and social analysis with no narrative cast of its own -- every entity is category Reference, per editorial policy's treatise guidance. As the automation queue's own note anticipated ("Named Americans and Europeans; watch place-versus-person"), this book names a large and varied real cast -- American founders and Presidents, legal commentators, colonial historians, geographers and travelers on Native American subjects, and a wide scatter of European philosophers and men of letters cited singly across Volume II's many short chapters -- but remains reference-light relative to its size (2258 paragraphs, ~1547 distinct capitalized word forms in a full-book sweep, comparable to The Wealth of Nations's ~1463 despite being somewhat longer). Volume I's long historical and legal chapters, especially the 372-paragraph chapter on the future condition of the three races (Native Americans, whites, and enslaved Africans) and the 238-paragraph Federal Constitution chapter, carry almost the entire named cast; Volume II's 75 short chapters name comparatively few people, mostly single scattered classical or literary citations. Five person-versus-place or namesake checks were made and resolved cleanly from context, without needing the escape hatch: bare "Washington" (the person dominates seven-to-one over the one reference to the city sharing his name, and is bound accordingly, with the minority place-reference documented rather than silently absorbed), Philip of Macedon vs. Metacom ("King Philip"; the two never share a literal name-string in this book), Jacques-Louis David the painter vs. the biblical King David (the biblical king is never separately named here), and two place names that are not people at all -- "Peter"/"Francis" (parts of the St. Peter's and St. Francis rivers) and "Chester" (a New York county). Bare "Caesar" is left unbound throughout, used only as a generic nickname or byword for seizing power, never as a specific narrative reference. Edition divergence in this book is markedly smaller than in Leviathan or The Wealth of Nations: only two spelling variants were found and aliased ("Sylla"/"Sulla", "Sevigne"/"Sévigné"). Both editions were read and reviewed independently.
